summary: A response from Peggy Karp of MITRE to a request for comments on computer-based instruction over the network. She attaches excerpts from an internal MITRE status report describing the company's ARPANET studies. These cover how MITRE joined the network through a terminal IMP in 1971 and how it planned to use network resources, including instructional ones.

plainLanguage.summary: A person was asked what her company was doing with computer lessons over the network. She answered by sharing parts of her company's progress report.

questions: computer based instruction on the arpanet
what did mitre do on the arpanet
subtitle: MITRE's plans to teach via the ARPANET using remote systems

tldr.problem: MITRE wanted to expand teaching capabilities by using computer-based instruction systems available on the ARPANET rather than building everything locally.
tldr.mechanism: MITRE joined the ARPANET in September 1971 and proposed using remote graphics systems, AI-based teaching tools, and storage resources across the network to extend its TICCIT computer-assisted instruction system.
tldr.outcome: MITRE demonstrated how to connect remote systems like the Culler-Fried graphics system at UCSB and AI tools like LOGO and SCHOLAR to a local education system, showing distributed instruction was possible.

today: RFC 321 is a historical record of early computer-based instruction experiments on the ARPANET. MITRE's vision of distributed learning systems anticipated modern online education, though it remains unknown how far these 1972 experiments progressed.

sections.title: MITRE's Network Teaching Work
sections.content: In March 1972, Peggy Karp of MITRE described the company's research into using the ARPANET to enhance computer-based instruction. MITRE had joined the ARPANET in September 1971 with a Terminal Interface Message Processor (TIP) and was exploring how network resources could extend the capabilities of its TICCIT system—a time-shared interactive computer controlled information television system used for teaching.
sections.plainLanguage: MITRE plugged into the ARPANET to see if the network could help it teach kids with computers.

sections.title: The Three-Part Approach
sections.content: MITRE organized its network research into three task areas. The first was to build up ARPANET usage within the company. The second involved conducting data sharing experiments with software at multiple network sites. The third, and the focus of this RFC, was to demonstrate how TICCIT's teaching capabilities could be extended by drawing on ARPANET resources, turning TICCIT into the hub of a distributed system.
sections.plainLanguage: The team split its work into three areas: using the network more, sharing data, and connecting the teaching computer to distant helpers.

sections.title: Graphics, AI Tools, and Shared Resources
sections.content: MITRE's demonstration focused on three specific capabilities. First, it extended TICCIT's mathematics teaching by connecting to the Culler-Fried graphics system at the University of California at Santa Barbara over the network, allowing students to interact with complex graphics remotely. Second, it planned to supplement TICCIT's lessons with AI-powered teaching systems: SCHOLAR, a question-answering system available at BBN, and LOGO, a graphics-based programming language from MIT designed to teach problem-solving. Third, MITRE proposed using remote storage and computing resources on the network to store student records and run statistical analysis on student progress.
sections.plainLanguage: MITRE connected three useful tools: a system at a far-away university for drawing graphs, smart teaching programs at other computers that could answer questions, and computers that could store grades.

sections.title: Progress and Plans
sections.content: By March 1972, MITRE had made progress on graphics but encountered technical challenges—the remote IMLAC graphics display available to MITRE had limited memory. The team had successfully used SCHOLAR over the network and was coordinating with MIT, where Seymour Papert was developing LOGO with a display turtle for remote access. MITRE planned to offer sample mathematics and computer science courses to demonstrate the feasibility of using distributed network resources for instruction, though work on the storage and statistical analysis component had not yet begun.
sections.plainLanguage: MITRE had partial success: the graphics didn't work perfectly yet because the equipment was old, but the smart teaching programs were working, and they were making plans to teach full courses.
